title: Running an AI demo agent on your real product: demo environment, complex UIs and PII
summary: Live app, demo tenant or clone? How an AI demo agent runs on your product, handles drag and drop and maps, keeps PII out, and what engineering sets up.
body_markdown:
Most teams run an AI demo agent on a separate demo tenant of their real product: the same app and the same release customers use, signed in as a demo account that holds safe sample data. You do not need a cloned copy of your app, and you should never point the agent at an account with real customer data; Karumi runs on a demo tenant of your live product or, if you prefer, on an offline replica with fake data.


Karumi is an AI demo agent: an autonomous agent that shows a buyer your real product live, by voice or chat, and answers questions as it goes. This guide answers what engineering and security teams ask before an agent drives their product: where it runs, how it copes with complex screens, how PII stays out and what they must set up. Product facts come from Karumi's own documentation, checked November 2026.


## Do you need a separate demo environment, your live app or a clone?


You need a place where any buyer may see anything. That rules out your production account with real customers. It leaves four options.


Option What the agent drives Good when Watch for


Demo tenant of your live product Your production app, signed in to a workspace with sample data You want buyers to see the current release and ask anything Keep the sample data clean, and know that a release can break a step


Staging copy A test deployment of your app You want to show features before they ship Staging changes and breaks more often than production


Offline replica A captured copy of your app with fake data, driven live in a browser You want data that never changes and a demo no release can break It does not show new screens until the change is folded in


Your customers' production account Real customer records Never Every screen can show PII


Karumi's launch checklist says it plainly: the agent needs "a tenant or workspace of your product filled with realistic data that is safe for prospects to see. Never point the agent at an account with customer data."


The offline replica is not a recording or a tour. Karumi captures your product with demo data, and the agent still clicks through it live while it talks. Karumi re-scans the product every day and folds real changes into the replica, as[how Karumi works](https://karumi.ai/blog/how-does-karumi-work) explains. One capture can also show different sample data to different audiences, for example a gym, a clinic or a salon, without a second copy.


## What does engineering need to provide?


Less than most teams expect. The agent signs in through your login page and works in the interface, like a person. It needs no database access and no SDK in your product.


1. **A demo account on a safe tenant.** One account on one tenant, with realistic sample data. Several agents, or several languages of one agent, can share it. A language can point at its own tenant.
2. **A way to sign in.** You save the login as a login profile. Supported types are email and password, Google, a magic link or a code sent by email. Add an authenticator app secret if the account uses one. If your product uses SSO or another second factor, talk to Karumi before you set a launch date.
3. **Network access.** If your product, or the demo or staging environment, only accepts known IP addresses, add Karumi's egress addresses. Karumi sends them on request.
4. **A list of no-go areas.** Billing, account deletion, admin screens. These go into the agent's instructions.
5. **The place the demo opens.** A demo link needs nothing. The demo button, the chat bar and the inline start screen are each one snippet on your page. Add the domains that embed the demo to your allowed list, and allow the microphone if your site sends a Permissions-Policy header.
6. **For demos inside your app only.** A server call that issues a short-lived identity token for each signed-in user, so the chat knows who they are.


Karumi then maps the product, reads your docs and drafts the demo flows. A first version is usually ready within a few hours of getting a login and your docs. For the mapping step in detail, read[how Karumi learns your product](https://karumi.ai/blog/how-does-karumi-learn-my-product) .


## How does an AI agent handle drag and drop, maps and other complex screens?


The hard part of a complex UI is finding the right thing to act on after the screen changes. Here is how Karumi does it.


- **It remembers what an element is, not where it was.** Each step of a demo flow stores the element's label, its role on the page and what sits around it. On replay, the agent looks for that element on the live page, the way you find the Save button after it moves.
- **It has more actions than a click.** A step can type, hover, scroll, upload a file, or drag one element onto another, such as a card into a new column or a field onto a form.
- **It can act where there is no button.** Maps, charts, canvases and whiteboards draw their content, so there is no element to find. For these, a step acts on a position on the screen, and it can press, hold and release the mouse to pan a map or draw a shape.
- **It knows the product's layout.** Because Karumi mapped the product first, the agent knows which page it is on and what that page is for. It can find its way to a screen that is not in a planned flow.
- **It is tested before buyers see it.** Karumi tests each demo flow against your product. A setting keeps a flow that failed its latest test out of live demos until it passes again.


In our experience, the reliable way to show a map or a drag-and-drop builder is a recorded demo flow for the key moves: zoom to a region, open a layer, drop a pin, move a card. The agent narrates the flow, stops when the buyer interrupts, and answers questions over the live screen. Free improvisation on a canvas is harder than on forms and buttons, for any agent.


A captured tour cannot do this at all. A click-through of a map is a set of still images, so the buyer cannot pan or drop a pin. See[live vs pre-recorded AI demo agents](https://karumi.ai/blog/live-vs-pre-recorded-ai-demo-agents) for a 2-minute test that shows the difference.


## How do you keep PII and the wrong screens out of a live demo?


Stack these layers.


Layer What it stops


A demo tenant with sample data Real customer records on screen


An offline replica with fake data Any change to real data, and surprise pop-ups or releases


Approved flows and no-go areas The agent opening billing, admin or settings pages you did not approve


An isolated browser on a demo account The demo touching your customers' accounts


Email checks and blocked domains Fake, personal or competitor emails starting a demo


A logged-out guard A broken demo when the login fails: buyers see an unavailable screen, and your team gets a Slack and email alert


The buyer's own data needs care too. For each session, Karumi stores the email and form answers, the transcript, a recording when one exists, the insights it extracted, and technical data such as device and approximate location. An Editor can delete a session, which removes it and its transcript from Karumi. The browser conversion events that reach your page carry only a session ID and an audience ID, never personal data. On the Enterprise plan, Karumi lists SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 and GDPR, and on-premise deployment ([pricing](https://karumi.ai/pricing) ). More detail is in[Karumi's enterprise features](https://karumi.ai/blog/enterprise-features-karumi) .


## Can the agent run inside your app, on the user's own account?


Yes. For onboarding, the same agent runs as a chat inside your product. Your server identifies the signed-in user with a short-lived token, so their progress follows them across devices.


The chat can run a recorded demo flow on the page, and you choose who does the work:


1. **The assistant does it all.** It clicks and types while the user presses Next.
2. **The user does it, with help.** The assistant points at each step, and a "Do it for me" button hands a step back.
3. **The user does all of it.** The assistant navigates, scrolls and points, and clicks nothing.


By default the assistant asks first, with a "Show me" card, and nothing moves until the user agrees. Here the user sees their own data, in their own account, so no demo tenant is needed.


## How do a buyer's questions change what the agent shows?


The agent follows the buyer, not a fixed path. It picks the demo flow that matches what the buyer said, and the buyer can interrupt at any point, by voice or by typing. After an interruption, the new question comes first, and the agent resumes the old walkthrough only when the buyer asks. To see it, ask an agent on the[demo gallery](https://karumi.ai/demos) for something off the main path.


## How do other AI demo tools handle the demo environment?


Vendors take three approaches. Each one is a fair choice for some teams.


Approach Examples What the buyer sees


Captured demos and sandboxes Navattic, Supademo, Walnut Copies of your screens, built in the vendor's editor


Demo data layered on your native product Saleo Your product, with demo data placed into it


An agent on a demo account in a real browser Karumi, Floe Your product, live


Sources, checked November 2026: Navattic lists sandbox demos on its Growth plan and offline demos on Enterprise ([Navattic pricing](https://www.navattic.com/pricing) ). Supademo lists guided HTML demos and sandbox demos on Enterprise ([Supademo pricing](https://supademo.com/pricing) ). Walnut embeds interactive demos in a shared deal room, "without a single screen-share" ([Walnut pricing](https://www.walnut.io/pricing/) ). Saleo says its AI Demo Agent is "Powered by Live demo data" ([Saleo announcement](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/saleo-launches-ai-demo-agent-fully-autonomous-b2b-product-demos-302664802.html) ). Floe drives your product in a real browser with a demo account ([Floe](https://floe.so/compare/best-ai-demo-agents) ).


Captured demos are the safest for PII, because nothing is live, but someone re-captures them after each release. A live agent shows the current product, but it needs the tenant and the guardrails above. For a side by side with Saleo, read[Karumi vs Saleo](https://karumi.ai/blog/karumi-vs-saleo) .


## FAQ


### Does an AI demo agent need access to my production database?


No. Karumi's agent signs in through your login page with a demo account and works in the interface, like a person. Nothing connects to your database or your API.


### Can the agent change data in my product during a demo?


Yes, it clicks and types like a user, so it can create records in the demo tenant. List the actions it must never take in its instructions, and use a tenant you can reset. On an offline replica, nothing reaches your product at all.


### What if our product signs in with SSO?


A login profile supports email and password, Google, a magic link and an email code, plus an authenticator app secret. For SSO or another kind of second factor, contact Karumi before you set a launch date.


### Will the demo break when we ship a release?


On a live tenant, Karumi tests the demo flows and can keep a failing flow out of live demos until it passes again. On an offline replica, a release cannot break the demo, and real changes are folded in after the daily re-scan.


### How long does setup take?


A first version is usually ready within a few hours of giving Karumi a login and your docs. Most teams spend a few days refining the demo flows before they go live.


See it work on real products before you set up your own: try a live demo at[karumi.ai/demos](https://karumi.ai/demos) .
